mission: Produce a working, version-controlled Claude harness for one real project: a CLAUDE.md of permanent rules, a primer.md that is rewritten every session, a skills/ folder of reusable workflows, and at least one hook that self-corrects behaviour. Done means a fresh Claude session loads the harness, acts on it, and a before/after A-B test on three repeated tasks shows the harness version is measurably leaner or more correct than a bare session.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A production agent engineer does not 'write a CLAUDE.md'. Following Richmond Alake's split that lindavivah relays, they separate three disciplines and build each deliberately: context engineering (signal/noise inside the window), memory engineering (what is retrieved, forgotten, evolved across sessions), and harness engineering (the scaffold code around the model). They treat the harness as code with tests: an eval set of representative tasks, an A-B harness that runs the same task with and without each component, and a metric (tokens, tool calls, pass rate). They ablate rules the way Boris Cherny's team does with simple mode, keeping only what earns its place.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Anthropic's own Claude Code docs on CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks and memory; Boris Cherny's published personal CLAUDE.md (plan-first, subagents, tasks/lessons.md, verification standard) that keshavsuki and evolving.ai describe; the primer.md + memory.sh + git-hook pattern keshavsuki shows; Graphify's repo for the knowledge-graph retrieval layer chase.h.ai demos; and your own last 20-50 session transcripts, which are the ground truth for what your harness actually needs.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Claude Code with a real git repo; a CLAUDE.md (rules), primer.md (session state, rewritten end-of-session), skills/ as markdown workflows, .claude/hooks/ for SessionStart context injection and PostToolUse guards; a memory.sh that injects last-5-commits + modified files at launch; Graphify (`/graphify .`) for query-before-read retrieval; a tiny A-B script that runs three fixed tasks with and without the harness and logs token counts and tool-call counts.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: An A-B test on three repeated tasks (harness vs bare session) where the harness version wins on at least one hard metric (fewer tokens, fewer tool calls, or a correctness check passing). A second, independent Claude session reading only the committed harness reproduces the intended behaviour without extra instruction. Boris Cherny's own ablation discipline is the oracle for whether each rule helps.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as an agent-harness engineer, not a prompt writer. For the repo at <path>, build me a three-layer Claude harness and prove it works. Layer 1 context: a CLAUDE.md of permanent, imperative rules distilled from my last 20 session transcripts at <transcripts path>, not generic advice. Layer 2 memory: a primer.md you rewrite at end of every session (current status, what changed, next up, blockers) plus a memory.sh that injects last-5-commits and modified files at launch. Layer 3 harness: a skills/ folder with at least two reusable workflows I actually repeat, and one .claude hook that self-corrects a behaviour I keep correcting. Then build an A-B test: pick three tasks I do often, run each with and without the harness, and log tokens and tool calls for both. Keep only harness components whose removal measurably hurts the A-B result, ablating the rest the way Boris Cherny's simple mode does. Return the committed files, the A-B numbers, and a short list of what you could not verify and why.

one_shot:
You are an agent-harness engineer. Your job is not to write a better prompt; it is to build and prove a three-layer harness around Claude for one real project. Stance: adversarial about your own work, imperative in your writing, no marketing language.

Context you must gather first: the repo at the path I give you, my recent Claude Code session transcripts (search ~/.claude/projects for this project), any existing CLAUDE.md or primer.md, and the three disciplines Richmond Alake names (context = signal/noise in the window; memory = retrieve/forget/evolve across sessions; harness = the scaffold code). Treat Boris Cherny's published CLAUDE.md as the reference pattern: plan-first, subagents for hard problems, every correction becomes a rule in tasks/lessons.md, never mark done without proving it works. Treat Graphify as the optional retrieval layer (build a graph once, query before opening raw files).

Hard constraints: every rule you write must trace to evidence in my transcripts or to a named Anthropic doc feature, never to generic best-practice. Do not invent workflow I do not actually repeat. Do not add a component you cannot A-B test. Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. Write files, do not just describe them. Touch only this repo.

Ordered deliverables: (1) CLAUDE.md of permanent imperative rules, each annotated with the transcript evidence that justifies it. (2) primer.md seeded with current project state, plus a one-line CLAUDE.md rule to rewrite it at session end. (3) memory.sh that prints last-5-commits, modified files and current branch, wired via a SessionStart hook. (4) skills/ with at least two reusable workflows I repeat, each a standalone markdown file. (5) at least one .claude hook that self-corrects a behaviour I keep correcting (name the behaviour). (6) an A-B test script: three fixed tasks, each run with and without the harness, logging token count and tool-call count. (7) the A-B results table.

Built-in gap analysis: before you finish, list every claim you have not verified (does the hook actually fire? does memory.sh run on this OS? did the A-B test use the same task text both arms?), and fill what you can by running it. If a transcript is missing, say so and derive rules from what exists rather than guessing.

Self-questions you must answer in writing before finishing: Which of my rules would a second Claude session misread? Which component, if deleted, would the A-B test not notice (ablate it)? Is primer.md state, not a changelog? Does any skill duplicate a rule already in CLAUDE.md? Did I conflate context, memory and harness anywhere? Does the hook have a bypass? Is any number in the A-B table from a run that actually happened?

Stop conditions: stop and ask me only if the repo has no git history or no readable transcripts. Otherwise proceed end-to-end.

Return format: a markdown report with the file tree of what you created, the A-B results table (task, arm, tokens, tool calls), the ablation decisions (component / kept or cut / why), and a final 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the harness files; print the commit hash.

steps.title: Ground truth from transcripts
steps.goal: Derive what the harness must do from real session evidence, not advice.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth before building anything. Locate my Claude Code session transcripts for this project (search under ~/.claude/projects for the directory matching this repo). Read the 15-30 most recent sessions. Extract, with a count for each: (a) corrections I repeat to Claude (the same complaint more than once), (b) context I paste or re-explain most sessions, (c) tasks I run more than twice, (d) mistakes that cost a retry. Also read any existing CLAUDE.md and primer.md and note what they already cover. Classify every finding into Richmond Alake's three buckets: context (belongs in the window every session), memory (must persist across sessions), harness (needs scaffold code or a hook). Output a table: finding, count, bucket, proposed component. Do not propose anything with a count of 1 unless it is safety- or money-touching. This table is the spec for every later step.
steps.expect: A table of 10-25 evidence-backed findings, each with an occurrence count and a context/memory/harness classification, plus a note on what the existing setup already covers.
steps.audit: Re-open two transcripts at random and confirm each finding you listed actually appears there with the count you claimed. Fail if any finding has no transcript backing or if you proposed a component for a count-1, non-safety item. On fail, drop the unbacked findings and recount.

steps.title: Write CLAUDE.md (context layer)
steps.goal: Produce permanent imperative rules, each justified by step 1 evidence.
steps.prompt: Using the step 1 table, write CLAUDE.md for this repo. Rules only, imperative voice, no explanations of what Claude is. Model the structure on Boris Cherny's pattern: plan before touching code; use subagents for hard problems to keep the main context clean; every correction becomes a rule; never mark a task done without proving it (tests or a behaviour diff against main). For each rule add a trailing comment `# evidence: <finding, count>` tying it to step 1. Keep the whole file under 200 lines. Put only context-bucket findings here; memory and harness findings go to later steps. Explicitly do NOT include a rule unless step 1 gave it a count or it is a safety/money guardrail. End the file with one rule: 'At end of session, rewrite primer.md completely (status, what changed, next up, blockers).'
steps.expect: A CLAUDE.md under 200 lines, every rule annotated with its evidence tag, ending with the primer.md rewrite rule.
steps.audit: Grep the file for rules without an `# evidence:` tag or safety justification; each one is a fail and must be cut. Confirm line count < 200. Confirm no rule restates a generic 'handle errors' platitude.

steps.title: Memory layer: primer.md + memory.sh
steps.goal: Make session state persist and git state auto-inject at launch.
steps.prompt: Build the memory layer keshavsuki describes. (1) Write primer.md seeded with the project's current status, what changed recently (from git log), next up, blockers, open questions. It is a snapshot, not a log. (2) Write memory.sh that prints the last 5 commits (`git log --oneline -5`), modified files (`git status --short`), and current branch, so a new session sees what changed before I speak. (3) Wire memory.sh into a SessionStart hook in .claude/settings.json (or settings.local.json) so it runs at launch, output captured to context. Do not duplicate anything already stated in CLAUDE.md. Keep primer.md under 150 lines.
steps.expect: primer.md (state snapshot), memory.sh (executable, prints commits/files/branch), and a SessionStart hook entry that runs it.
steps.audit: Run memory.sh in a shell and confirm it prints without error on this OS. Confirm the hook JSON is valid (parse it). Fail if memory.sh errors, if the hook JSON is malformed, or if primer.md is a changelog rather than current state. On fail, fix before continuing.

steps.title: Skills: reusable workflows
steps.goal: Turn repeated tasks from step 1 into standalone skill files.
steps.prompt: Take the two highest-count 'task I repeat' findings from step 1 and write each as a standalone skill markdown file under skills/<name>/SKILL.md. Each skill must be self-contained: a one-line trigger description, the ordered steps, the exact commands or file paths it touches, and a done-check. Do not personify ('act as an expert'); define the workflow and its end state, following angus.sewell's point that AI is good at specific workflows with clear instructions and a clear end state, not personas. Each skill must name the real tools and paths from this repo. Do not write a skill for a task that appears only once.
steps.expect: Two or more SKILL.md files, each standalone, trigger + steps + commands + done-check, naming this repo's real tools/paths.
steps.audit: For each skill, verify you could hand it to a fresh agent with no other context and it would run. Fail any skill that references a variable or path defined only in your head, or that duplicates a CLAUDE.md rule. On fail, inline the missing context or merge into CLAUDE.md.

steps.title: Self-correcting hook
steps.goal: Mechanically enforce one behaviour you keep correcting.
steps.prompt: Pick the single highest-count correction from step 1 that can be enforced mechanically (e.g. deleting files, unbounded output, skipping tests). Write a hook in .claude/ that enforces it, modelled on jens.heitmann's daily hooks: for a deletion risk, a PreToolUse hook that moves files to a staging folder instead of deleting; for a verification gap, a Stop hook that checks tests ran. Make the hook fail loudly, not silently. Register it in settings. Document in one line what behaviour it guards and how to bypass it deliberately if ever needed.
steps.expect: One working hook file plus its settings registration, guarding a named step-1 behaviour, with a documented deliberate-bypass path.
steps.audit: Trigger the guarded behaviour in a scratch test and confirm the hook fires and blocks or redirects it. Fail if the hook is silent, if it never fires, or if it has an accidental bypass. On fail, fix the trigger condition and retest.

steps.title: A-B test the harness
steps.goal: Prove each component earns its place; ablate the rest.
steps.prompt: Build the proof. Choose three tasks I actually run on this repo (from step 1). For each task, run it twice with identical task text: arm A in a session with the full harness loaded, arm B in a bare session (use `claude --system-prompt` minimal or an empty CLAUDE.md). Log tokens used and tool-call count for both arms. Then run an ablation: remove each harness component (one rule group, the memory layer, each skill, the hook) one at a time and re-run the most sensitive task; if removal does not change the metric, mark that component for deletion. Produce (1) an A-B table: task, arm, tokens, tool calls; (2) an ablation table: component, metric with / without, keep or cut. Delete the components you marked cut and note it.
steps.expect: An A-B results table and an ablation table; the harness trimmed to only components whose removal hurt a metric.
steps.audit: Confirm both arms of each A-B pair used byte-identical task text (diff them). Confirm every number came from a run that actually executed, not an estimate. Fail if any arm was imagined or if task text differed. Keep a component you cut only if it is a safety/money guardrail.

steps.title: Validate + gap report
steps.goal: Check against the oracles and report what is unverified.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Start a brand-new Claude session that reads ONLY the committed harness and give it one of the three tasks; confirm it behaves as the harness intends with no extra instruction. (2) Re-run the A-B test once more to confirm the harness arm still wins on at least one metric. (3) Enumerate every claim in your report and mark it verified / unverified / false with the evidence. (4) List what is still missing (a rule with no evidence, a skill never exercised, a hook not triggered in real use) ranked by impact, and fix the top two now. (5) Commit all harness files and print the commit hash. Return the final report with the file tree, both tables, the fresh-session result, and an 'Unverified and missing' section.
steps.expect: A fresh-session reproduction result, a re-run A-B confirmation, a verified/unverified/false claim ledger, and a committed harness with its hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the fresh session used no context beyond committed files. Confirm the commit actually exists (git show the hash). Fail if the harness arm does not win any metric, or if any 'verified' claim lacks evidence. On fail, state plainly that the harness did not beat baseline rather than massaging numbers.

gap_audit_prompt: Run this after the harness is built. Enumerate every claim in the build report as a numbered list: each rule in CLAUDE.md, each skill, the memory layer, the hook, and every A-B and ablation number. For each, mark VERIFIED (with the exact evidence: transcript line, command output, commit hash), UNVERIFIED (never actually exercised), or FALSE (contradicted by a run). Specifically re-check: does memory.sh run without error on this machine; does the SessionStart hook actually inject its output; did the self-correcting hook fire against a real trigger; did both A-B arms use identical task text; is every token/tool-call number from a real run. List all missing pieces: rules with no evidence tag, skills never run, components kept despite the ablation saying cut. Rank the gaps by impact on whether the harness actually helps. Fix the top three now and re-verify them. Report what you could not fix and exactly why (missing transcript, OS limitation, needs my input). Do not mark anything verified on the basis of 'it should work'.
self_questions: Did I separate context, memory and harness, or did I dump everything into CLAUDE.md?
Does every CLAUDE.md rule trace to a transcript finding with a count, or is some of it generic advice?
Is primer.md a current-state snapshot, or did I write a changelog?
Does memory.sh actually run on this OS, or did I assume it works?
Did the SessionStart hook actually inject context, or did I only register it?
Did the self-correcting hook fire against a real trigger, or only in theory?
Did both A-B arms use byte-identical task text?
Is any A-B or ablation number from a run that did not actually happen?
Which component would the ablation say to cut, and did I cut it?
Would a second Claude session reading only the committed files reproduce the behaviour?
Did any skill duplicate a rule already in CLAUDE.md?
Did I keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines and primer.md under 150?
Does the hook have an accidental bypass that defeats its purpose?
Did I ever personify a skill instead of defining its workflow and end state?
validation_oracles: A fresh Claude session reading only the committed harness performs one of the three test tasks correctly with no extra instruction.
The A-B test shows the harness arm beating the bare arm on at least one hard metric (tokens, tool calls, or a correctness check) across the three tasks.
memory.sh runs on the target machine and its SessionStart hook output appears in a new session's context.
The self-correcting hook demonstrably fires and blocks or redirects its guarded behaviour in a scratch test.
The ablation table shows every retained component (except safety/money guardrails) changes a metric when removed.
failure_modes: Generic CLAUDE.md: rules copied from blog posts with no evidence tag. Tell: rules you cannot tie to a transcript. Fix: cut everything without an `# evidence:` tag or safety reason.
primer.md becomes a diary: it grows and logs history instead of snapshotting current state. Tell: it keeps getting longer. Fix: rewrite from scratch each session, keep under 150 lines.
Hook registered but never fires: wrong event or matcher. Tell: the guarded behaviour still happens. Fix: trigger it in a scratch test and correct the matcher.
A-B theatre: arms used different task text or numbers were estimated. Tell: suspiciously clean wins. Fix: diff the task text, require real run logs.
Everything kept: ablation run but nothing cut because removal was never actually tested. Tell: ablation table has no 'cut' rows. Fix: re-run the sensitive task with each component removed.
Context/memory/harness conflated: skills restate CLAUDE.md rules, memory holds things that belong in the window. Tell: duplication across files. Fix: re-bucket using Alake's three definitions.
memory.sh breaks on the OS: assumed bash/git layout. Tell: errors at launch. Fix: run it and handle the real shell/paths.
agent_direction: Reach first for transcript search (glob ~/.claude/projects for this repo's dir) and git log; these are your evidence base, do not skip to writing rules. Cache the step-1 findings table; every later step reads it. Spawn a sub-agent only for the A-B runs so each arm starts with a clean context, and pass it byte-identical task text for both arms. Run memory.sh and the hook for real before claiming they work; never mark a mechanical component verified from reasoning alone. Stop and ask the user only if there is no git history or no readable transcripts for this project. Return a single markdown report plus the committed harness files: CLAUDE.md, primer.md, memory.sh, .claude/settings*.json, skills/*/SKILL.md, and any hook script. Put the A-B table, ablation table, fresh-session reproduction result and an 'Unverified and missing' section in the report, and print the commit hash. Do not publish anything outside the repo. If the harness arm fails to beat baseline, say so plainly; a null result is a valid, reportable outcome here.

one_shot:
You are an interactive-installation engineer building one real-time, body-reactive visual with MediaPipe and TouchDesigner. Stance: ship something that runs live and survives other people's bodies, not a screen-recorded demo. No marketing language.

Context: MediaPipe Tasks gives you HandLandmarker (21 points/hand), PoseLandmarker (33) and FaceLandmarker (468); pick one to start. TouchDesigner receives external data cleanly over OSC (python-osc) or, for lower latency, a Shared Memory CHOP. The @blankensmithing MediaPipe TD plugin exists if you prefer it to rolling your own transport. Reference work: pepepepebrick's hand-tracked spider-web audio-visual system, the DATLAB Classifier TOX (datlabnyc.com/classified) that trains a classifier on any CHOP data, and FreeMoCap for full-body 3D later. Landmark jitter is the enemy; a one-euro filter is the standard fix.

Hard constraints: 30fps+ under live tracking on a laptop webcam; end-to-end latency (gesture to pixel) must be measured, not assumed; the project must open and run on a second machine from the committed repo. Name real landmark indices, real TD operators, real file paths. Do not claim it works until it has run with a second person in the frame.

Ordered deliverables: (1) a mapping design doc: which landmark indices drive which visual parameters, smoothing and dead-zones, lost-tracking fallback, and one discrete gesture that triggers a state change. (2) the MediaPipe capture script (webcam -> landmarks -> OSC/SharedMem). (3) the TouchDesigner .toe: a GPU particle or instancing system driven by the incoming CHOP channels, with the one-euro filter applied. (4) a gesture classifier on the CHOP data for the discrete trigger (DATLAB TOX or a small sklearn model). (5) a latency + fps measurement. (6) a recorded clip and a second-person test report. (7) a run-on-another-machine packaging note.

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what you have not verified - does it hold 30fps with two hands in frame; does the gesture fire for someone else; does the .toe open clean on a fresh install; is the latency number from a real timestamp. Fill what you can by running it.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Which landmark indices am I actually using and why those? Is my smoothing hiding real motion or only jitter? What happens when tracking drops mid-gesture? Does the classifier generalise beyond my own hand? Is my fps measured under load or idle? Did I hardcode an absolute path that breaks on another machine? Is OSC dropping packets at high landmark rates?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if no webcam or no TouchDesigner is available. Otherwise build end-to-end.

Return format: a markdown report with the design doc, a file tree, the latency/fps table, the second-person test notes, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the capture script, the .toe and any classifier model; print the commit hash. One more discipline: treat the webcam frame itself as untrusted and variable. Different cameras expose different fields of view, white balance and frame rates, so normalise the landmark coordinate space (0-1 relative to frame) before mapping, and log the camera's actual resolution and fps alongside every performance number. When you report that a gesture works, name the exact lighting, distance from camera and hand orientation it was tested under, because a mapping tuned at arm's length in daylight often collapses at a desk under a lamp, and the design doc's thresholds must say which condition they assume.

steps.title: Ground truth: landmarks + transport
steps.goal: Confirm MediaPipe and the TD transport actually work before designing anything.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth. (1) Stand up MediaPipe Tasks Python on the webcam for your chosen tracker (HandLandmarker 21 / PoseLandmarker 33 / FaceLandmarker 468). Print the raw landmark array and confirm the indices match Google's diagram (e.g. hand index-finger tip = landmark 8, wrist = 0). (2) Open TouchDesigner and get ONE number flowing from Python into a CHOP, via OSC (python-osc -> OSC In CHOP) or a Shared Memory CHOP. Move your hand and watch the CHOP value change. (3) Measure the raw landmark update rate (Hz) and note CPU/GPU load. Document the exact MediaPipe model file, the transport choice, the port, and the landmark-index-to-channel map. Do not design visuals yet; this step only proves the pipe carries live data with correct indices.
steps.expect: Live landmark values printing with verified indices, at least one value flowing into a TD CHOP and visibly tracking motion, and a measured update rate.
steps.audit: Cross-check three landmark indices against Google's official diagram by moving that body part and confirming the right channel moves. Fail if indices are guessed or if the CHOP does not update live. On fail, fix the index map or transport before step 2.

steps.title: Mapping design doc
steps.goal: Decide the landmark-to-parameter mapping, smoothing and fallbacks on paper first.
steps.prompt: Write the mapping design doc before building visuals. Specify, as a table: each visual parameter you will drive (e.g. particle emission rate, force field position, color hue) and the exact landmark index/derived value that drives it (e.g. hand openness = distance landmarks 4-8; position = landmark 9 x/y). Define smoothing: a one-euro filter per channel with starting min-cutoff and beta values. Define dead-zones so resting hands do not twitch the visual. Define the lost-tracking fallback (freeze last value? fade out? which?). Define exactly ONE discrete gesture (e.g. pinch = landmarks 4-8 distance below threshold) that triggers a state change, and what state it toggles. Reference pepepepebrick's approach where proximity modulates sound/visual as a model. This doc is the contract step 3 and 4 must satisfy.
steps.expect: A design doc with a parameter->landmark table, per-channel smoothing params, dead-zones, a lost-tracking fallback, and one defined discrete gesture with its threshold and effect.
steps.audit: Check every visual parameter has exactly one defined driver and every driver is a real landmark index or derived value from step 1. Fail if any mapping is vague ('hand controls particles') or references an index you did not verify. On fail, make it specific.

steps.title: Build the reactive visual
steps.goal: Implement the TD GPU visual driven by the smoothed channels.
steps.prompt: Implement the visual in TouchDesigner per the design doc. Build a GPU particle or instancing system (POPs or instancing geometry) whose parameters are driven by the incoming CHOP channels from step 1. Apply the one-euro filter (Filter/Lag CHOP or a custom one-euro) to each channel using the design-doc values. Implement the dead-zones and the lost-tracking fallback exactly as specified. Do not add parameters the design doc did not define. Keep the render path GPU-bound; avoid per-frame Python in the render loop. Save as a .toe with a relative, portable project folder structure (media and TOXes inside the project dir, no absolute paths).
steps.expect: A .toe where moving the tracked body part visibly and smoothly drives the specified visual parameters, with jitter removed and a working lost-tracking fallback.
steps.audit: Trigger lost tracking (cover the camera) and confirm the fallback behaves as designed, not a freeze-crash. Grep the .toe/project for absolute paths. Fail on absolute paths, on jitter that reads as noise, or on any undefined parameter. On fail, fix smoothing/paths.

steps.title: Gesture classifier
steps.goal: Make the discrete gesture fire reliably via a classifier, not a brittle threshold alone.
steps.prompt: Add the discrete-gesture trigger from the design doc as a classifier on the CHOP data, following the DATLAB Classifier approach zerospacelabs demos (train categories on CHOP channels, get a confidence score). Either use the DATLAB Classifier TOX (datlabnyc.com/classified) or train a small scikit-learn model on recorded landmark samples of the gesture vs not-gesture. Record at least 50 positive and 50 negative samples, including some from a second person's hand if available. Wire the classifier output so the gesture state change only fires above a confidence threshold with a short debounce to avoid flicker. Report the classifier's accuracy on a held-out set.
steps.expect: A trained classifier (TOX or sklearn model) firing the discrete gesture above a confidence threshold with debounce, plus a held-out accuracy number.
steps.audit: Test the gesture 10 times deliberately and 10 times with random motion; count false positives and false negatives. Fail if false-positive rate under random motion is high or if it never fires. On fail, add samples, raise the threshold, or lengthen the debounce.

steps.title: Measure latency + fps

steps.prompt: Measure performance under real conditions. (1) Frame rate: run the full pipeline (camera + MediaPipe + transport + TD render) with the tracked body part moving, and log TD's fps over 60 seconds; also log with two hands / full body in frame if relevant. (2) Latency: timestamp a sharp gesture (e.g. a clap or pinch) at the camera and the moment the visual responds, and compute end-to-end ms; repeat 10 times and report median. (3) Note CPU/GPU utilisation. Produce a table: condition, fps, median latency, dropped frames. State the hardware (CPU/GPU, webcam resolution/fps).
steps.expect: A performance table with measured fps (idle and loaded), median end-to-end latency over 10 trials, dropped-frame count, and the hardware spec.
steps.audit: Confirm fps was measured with motion and tracking active, not idle. Confirm latency is from real timestamps, not estimated from fps. Fail if fps < 30 under load or latency > ~100ms median; on fail, drop camera resolution, switch OSC->Shared Memory CHOP, or move Python work off the render thread, then re-measure.

steps.title: Second-person test + portability + gap report

Commit the capture script, .toe, classifier model and a requirements.txt; print the commit hash.

steps.audit: Confirm the .toe opened on the second machine from the repo with no manual rewiring. Confirm the second-person test actually happened (clip or notes). Fail if it only works for the author or only on the build machine. On fail, state that limitation plainly in the report.

gap_audit_prompt: Run after the pipeline is built. Works only for the author: classifier trained on one hand. Tell: a second person's gesture never fires. Fix: add second-person samples, raise threshold, debounce.

Fake real-time: fps looked fine but latency is high. Tell: visible lag between gesture and response. Fix: measure latency with paired timestamps; switch to Shared Memory CHOP; move Python off the render thread.
Broken on another machine: absolute paths or external media. Tell: .toe opens with missing-file errors. Fix: portable project folder, relative paths, requirements.txt.

They add a context-sufficiency check (the agent asks for missing context before acting, per angus.sewell's PM loop), they prefer structured storage over vector memory for factual business context (angus.sewell: 'most memory should be structured'), and they ablate: remove a component, re-run the eval, keep it only if removal hurts. Is any component's gain inside the noise band? Did I reach for a vector DB where structured storage would have been better and cheaper? Does the sufficiency gate actually fire on under-specified tasks? Is the generator-evaluator loop improving answers or just adding cost? What is my cost per correct answer, not just pass rate?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if there are no task logs to build an eval from. Otherwise proceed end to end.

Return format: a markdown report with the eval description, a scores table (baseline + each component + full system), the ablation table, the noise check, cost-per-correct-answer, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the eval set, the runner, and the component code; print the commit hash. One more discipline: report cost and latency alongside every eval score, not pass rate alone. A component that lifts the pass rate but triples tokens or doubles latency is a trade-off the reader must see stated explicitly, so each row of your scores table carries pass rate, cost per correct answer, and median latency. And when you grade with a model rather than a human, spot-check at least five of its judgements by hand per run, because an LLM grader that drifts quietly turns your whole oracle into noise and every downstream decision inherits that error.

steps.title: Build the eval (the oracle)
steps.goal: Author a held-out eval of real tasks before any architecture.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth: the eval. From my real task logs (at the path I give you), sample 30-50 representative tasks covering the real distribution, including the failure cases. For each, write the input and an EXPLICIT, objective pass/fail criterion a human could apply (not 'is it good' - e.g. 'answer cites the correct policy section', 'returns valid JSON with fields x,y,z', 'refuses when the record is missing'). Split: none of these will be used to tune prompts (held-out). Build a tiny runner that executes the current single-prompt system against all tasks and scores pass/fail. This eval is the oracle every later step is judged against; architecture changes that do not move it do not ship.
steps.expect: A committed eval set of 30-50 tasks, each with input and an objective pass/fail criterion, plus a runner that scores a system against it.
steps.audit: Hand 5 tasks' criteria to yourself and confirm two people would grade them identically (objective). Confirm the sample includes real failure cases, not just easy ones. Fail if criteria are subjective or the set is cherry-picked easy tasks. On fail, rewrite the criteria and resample.

steps.title: Baseline + noise floor
steps.goal: Score the single prompt and measure how noisy the eval is.
steps.prompt: Establish the baseline and the noise floor. (1) Run the current single-prompt system against the full eval and record the score - this is the number everything must beat. (2) Run the SAME system against the eval twice more (identical config) and record the variance between the three runs. This is your noise floor: any later improvement smaller than this variance is noise, not signal. Report both the baseline score and the run-to-run variance. If the variance is large (e.g. comparable to the gaps you expect from architecture), flag that the eval is too noisy and must be enlarged or criteria tightened before trusting any result.
steps.expect: A baseline eval score and a measured run-to-run variance (noise floor), with a flag if noise is too high to trust.
steps.audit: Confirm the three runs used identical config (only sampling randomness differs). Fail if variance is high and you proceed anyway. On fail, enlarge the eval or tighten criteria until noise is below the improvement you need to detect.

steps.title: Context pipeline + sufficiency gate
steps.goal: Engineer what enters the window and make the agent flag missing context.
steps.prompt: Add the context layer. Map what currently enters the context window for a task and from where. Then add a context-sufficiency gate following angus.sewell's PM loop: before acting, the agent checks whether it has enough context and, if not, flags exactly what is missing rather than guessing. Trim noise from the window (remove context that does not affect the eval). Re-run the full eval and record the new score and the delta vs baseline. Report how many tasks triggered the sufficiency gate and whether gating reduced wrong-but-confident answers. Keep this layer only if the delta exceeds the step-2 noise floor.
steps.expect: A context pipeline with a working sufficiency gate, an eval score + delta vs baseline, and a count of gated tasks.
steps.audit: Feed 3 deliberately under-specified tasks and confirm the gate fires and names the missing context. Confirm the delta exceeds the noise floor before keeping it. Fail if the gate never fires or the gain is within noise. On fail, fix the gate or drop the layer.

steps.title: Memory layer (structured first)
steps.goal: Persist what the system must recall, structured over vector.
steps.prompt: Add the memory layer, defaulting to STRUCTURED storage per angus.sewell ('most memory should be structured'; vector memory 'mostly lies'). Decide what must persist across sessions/requests (facts, prior decisions, entities) and store it in SQLite/Postgres or markdown with clear keys - not a vector DB. Add embeddings/semantic search ONLY for the subset of recall that is genuinely fuzzy (free-text similarity), and justify it against the eval. Wire retrieval of this memory into the context pipeline. Re-run the eval, record score and delta. Keep structured vs vector per which moves the eval, not per hype.
steps.expect: A persisted memory layer (structured by default), wired into context, with an eval score + delta and a stated structured-vs-vector decision.
steps.audit: Verify the memory actually persists across two separate runs (write in one, read in the next). Confirm any vector component is justified by an eval delta over structured. Fail if memory does not persist or vector was added without evidence. On fail, fix persistence or revert to structured.

steps.title: Retrieval + self-correction, each gated
steps.goal: Add RAG and a generator-evaluator loop only if the eval improves.
steps.prompt: Add the last two components, each gated on the eval. (1) Retrieval: if the feature needs external/domain knowledge, add hybrid retrieval + reranking over your docs; re-run the eval; keep ONLY if the delta beats the noise floor, else cut it. (2) Self-correction: add a generator-evaluator loop where a second pass critiques the first against the task criteria and revises; re-run the eval; measure both the score delta AND the added cost/latency. Report each component's delta and cost. A component that improves pass rate but triples cost per correct answer is a trade-off to state explicitly, not a silent win.
steps.expect: Retrieval and self-correction each with an eval delta and a cost/latency figure; components below the noise floor cut.
steps.audit: Confirm each kept component's delta exceeds the noise floor. Compute cost per correct answer with and without each. Fail if a component is kept on a within-noise gain or if cost tripled unacknowledged. On fail, cut it or state the trade-off.

steps.title: Ablation, noise re-check, gap report
steps.goal: Prove each retained component earns its place; report honestly.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Ablation: remove each retained component one at a time, re-run the full eval, and record the score without it; keep only components whose removal drops the score beyond the noise floor. (2) Full-system run: score the complete architecture vs the baseline and report the delta and cost per correct answer. (3) Noise re-check: confirm the best-vs-worst architecture gap exceeds run-to-run variance; if not, state that the result is not trustworthy. (4) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit the eval, runner and components; print the hash.
steps.expect: An ablation table, a full-system vs baseline comparison with cost per correct answer, a passing noise re-check, a claim ledger, and a committed system with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the full system beats baseline by more than the noise floor. Confirm no component survives only on a within-noise gain. Fail if the architecture does not beat baseline, or beats it only inside noise. On fail, report that plainly - a null result is valid.

gap_audit_prompt: Run after the architecture is built. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the eval's representativeness, each component's eval delta, the memory persistence, the retrieval and self-correction gains, the ablation decisions, and the noise check. Mark each VERIFIED (with the run numbers), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: are the eval criteria objective and was the set truly held out (no tuning on it); is every reported delta larger than the run-to-run variance; did I default to structured memory and justify any vector use; does the sufficiency gate actually fire on under-specified inputs; is cost per correct answer reported, not just pass rate; does the full system beat baseline beyond noise. List missing pieces: unrepresentative eval, within-noise gains kept, vector memory added on hype, unmeasured cost. Rank by impact on whether the architecture is a real improvement. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not mark any improvement verified if it is within the noise floor.
self_questions: Are my eval pass/fail criteria objective enough that two people grade them the same?
Is the eval set truly held out, or did I tune prompts on it?
Does the eval cover real traffic including failure cases, or only easy tasks?
Is any component's reported gain inside the run-to-run noise band?
Did I default to structured memory, or reach for a vector DB on hype?
Does the memory layer actually persist across separate runs?
Does the context-sufficiency gate fire on under-specified tasks?
Is the generator-evaluator loop improving answers or just adding cost?
What is my cost per correct answer, not just pass rate, for each component?
Does the full architecture beat baseline by more than the noise floor?
Did I ablate every component, and did I cut the ones removal did not hurt?
If the result is within noise, did I say so rather than claim a win?
validation_oracles: On the held-out eval, the full architecture beats the single-prompt baseline by more than the run-to-run variance, on a stated metric.
The ablation table shows every retained component drops the eval score when removed (beyond the noise floor); cut components do not.
The context-sufficiency gate fires on deliberately under-specified tasks and names the missing context.
The memory layer persists across two separate runs (write in one, read in the next), and any vector use is justified by an eval delta over structured storage.
Cost per correct answer is reported for the baseline and the full system, making any accuracy/cost trade-off explicit.
failure_modes: No eval, just vibes: changes judged by eyeballing. Tell: 'it feels better'. Fix: author a held-out eval with objective criteria first.
Tuning on the held-out set: prompts adjusted using eval feedback. Tell: great eval score, poor production. Fix: keep a sealed set never used for tuning.
Chasing noise: a within-variance gain treated as real. Tell: improvements smaller than run-to-run variance. Fix: measure the noise floor; require gains above it.
Vector memory by default: embeddings where structured recall was needed. Tell: memory 'lies', factual recall wrong. Fix: structured storage first, vector only where justified.
Self-correction cost blindness: loop improves pass rate but triples cost. Tell: latency and spend balloon. Fix: report cost per correct answer; state the trade-off.
Sufficiency gate that never fires: gate added but mis-wired. Tell: confident wrong answers on under-specified tasks. Fix: test with under-specified inputs, correct the trigger.
Component kept untested: added but never ablated. Tell: ablation table missing rows. Fix: remove each component, re-run, decide on evidence.
agent_direction: Reach first for the task logs to build the eval and the baseline; without the eval nothing else is measurable, so do not start adding components before it exists. Cache the eval set and the baseline + noise floor; every component step reads them. Add components one at a time and re-run the eval after each - never batch changes, or you cannot attribute the delta. Default memory to structured storage; only spawn the extra work of a vector/embedding layer when an eval delta justifies it. Compute cost per correct answer alongside pass rate on every run. Stop and ask the user only if there are no task logs to build an eval from. Return a markdown report (eval description, scores table, ablation table, noise check, cost per correct answer, 'Unverified and missing') plus the committed eval set, runner and component code; print the commit hash. If the architecture does not beat baseline beyond noise, report that as the finding - a null result is a valid, useful outcome.

mission: Separate working autonomous-agent patterns from demo-ware by building and stress-testing one narrow agent with real guardrails: a single task, one or two tools, fast feedback, hard budget and scope caps, persistent memory, and an adversarial test suite that tries to break it. Done means the agent completes its task unattended across a run, the guardrails demonstrably stop every adversarial case, and a logged review shows where it failed and what was pruned.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A builder who ships reliable agents, not demos, follows the pattern these entries converge on: narrow scope, fast feedback, cheap failure. They build guardrails BEFORE capability - kill switches, budget limits, scope allowlists, hard-coded risk rules the agent cannot override (raycfu's trading agent locks stop-losses in code). They add persistence so the agent does not repeat mistakes (structured memory over vector, per angus.sewell), a context-sufficiency gate so it asks before acting, and they test adversarially against edge cases and misalignment - knowing, per lizthedeveloper, that models can be evaluation-aware and a benchmark can look better than real behaviour. They log everything (PostHog-style observability) and keep fix decisions human.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Your own agent's task logs and the failure cases in them; angus.sewell's project-management loop (tasks table, context-sufficiency check, skill mining from paper trails) and structured-warehouse-as-memory pattern; raycfu's hard-coded-risk-limits-in-code pattern; the agentic-misalignment eval lizthedeveloper references (Anthropic's) and the evaluation-awareness caveat; a canary/budget environment you control; a disposable test target you own.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: A single-task agent in Claude Code or the Agent SDK with one or two tools; a scope allowlist on tool calls and outbound actions; a hard budget cap (token/$ and wall-clock) enforced in code, not prose; a kill switch; structured persistent memory (SQLite/markdown) of prior actions and mistakes; a context-sufficiency gate; an adversarial test suite (edge cases, ambiguous instructions, misalignment probes) with a canary; append-only audit logging of every tool call; a human review step for fixes.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The agent completes its narrow task unattended over a full run without exceeding budget or scope. The adversarial suite: every case either handled correctly or safely refused, with the guardrail that caught it named. The budget cap and kill switch demonstrably halt the agent when tripped. A control comparison: the same agent with guardrails removed fails the adversarial cases the guarded one passed, proving the guardrails, not luck, did the work.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a reliability engineer for autonomous agents, not a demo builder. Help me build ONE narrow agent and prove it is reliable, not impressive. Pick a single task with fast, cheap feedback and one or two tools. Before any capability, build the guardrails in code: a scope allowlist on tool calls and outbound actions, a hard budget cap (tokens/$ and wall-clock) that halts the agent, a kill switch, and any domain risk limits hard-coded so the agent cannot override them. Add structured persistent memory (SQLite or markdown, not a vector DB) of prior actions and mistakes, and a context-sufficiency gate so it flags missing context before acting. Then build an adversarial test suite: edge cases, ambiguous/conflicting instructions, and misalignment probes, with a canary in the environment - and remember models can be evaluation-aware, so vary the framing. Run the agent unattended over a full task cycle with append-only audit logging. Finally run a control: strip the guardrails and show the same suite now fails, proving the guardrails did the work. Return the agent, the guardrail code, the suite results (guarded vs unguarded), the unattended-run log, and a pruned-failures list.

one_shot:
You are a reliability engineer for autonomous agents. Your job is to build ONE narrow agent and prove it is reliable under stress, not to build an impressive demo. Stance: guardrails before capability; everything logged; fixes stay human. No marketing language.

Context and method: the pattern that works across the field is narrow scope, fast feedback, cheap failure; general agents with vague goals fail. Build guardrails first - raycfu hard-codes risk limits the agent cannot override; angus.sewell routes work through a tasks table with a context-sufficiency gate and mines skills from paper trails, and argues structured memory beats vector memory. lizthedeveloper's caveat is load-bearing: models can be evaluation-aware, so a clean benchmark can overstate real safety - vary adversarial framing and do not trust a single pass.

Hard constraints: single task, one or two tools; a scope allowlist and a hard budget cap (tokens/$ + wall-clock) enforced in code; a kill switch; structured persistent memory; a context-sufficiency gate; an adversarial suite with a canary; append-only audit logging of every tool call. Test only systems, accounts and keys you own. Name real tools, real caps, real paths. Do not claim reliability from one clean run.

Ordered deliverables: (1) the agent's charter - exact task, allowed tools, done-criteria, and what it must never do. (2) guardrail code: scope allowlist, budget cap that halts, kill switch, any hard-coded risk limits. (3) structured persistent memory of actions + mistakes, plus a context-sufficiency gate. (4) an adversarial test suite: edge cases, ambiguous/conflicting instructions, misalignment probes, each with varied framing and a canary. (5) an unattended full-run log with append-only audit of every tool call. (6) a guarded-vs-unguarded control: run the suite with guardrails on and off. (7) a pruned-failures list: what broke and what you removed or fixed.

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what is unverified - did the budget cap actually halt a run; did the kill switch work mid-action; did any adversarial case pass only because the agent recognised the test; is the memory actually preventing repeat mistakes. Fill what you can by running it.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Is the scope genuinely narrow, or did I smuggle in generality? Does the budget cap halt in code, or only ask nicely? Did the kill switch stop an action in flight? Could any adversarial pass be evaluation-awareness rather than real safety? Is memory structured, and does it stop a repeated mistake? Does the sufficiency gate fire on ambiguous tasks? In the unguarded control, did the suite actually fail - proving the guardrails did the work?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if the task cannot be scoped narrowly or there is no safe test target. Otherwise build end to end.

Return format: a markdown report with the charter, a file tree, the suite results table (case, guarded result, unguarded result, guardrail that caught it), the unattended-run summary, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the agent, guardrails, memory and suite; print the commit hash. One more discipline: log the agent's reasoning, not just its actions, so a post-run review can tell a correct refusal from a lucky one. For every tool call the audit log should record what the agent believed it was doing and why, which is what lets you distinguish real safety from evaluation-awareness when you re-read it. And keep the feedback loop fast and the blast radius small throughout: a task where a wrong action is cheap to detect and cheap to undo is the only setting in which running unattended is responsible, so state in the charter exactly how a bad action here would be caught and reversed.

steps.title: Charter: narrow the scope
steps.goal: Define one task, its tools, done-criteria, and hard nevers.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth: the charter. Pick ONE narrow task with fast, cheap feedback (e.g. 'draft replies to support emails matching these FAQs', 'triage new issues into labels'). Write: the exact task, the one or two tools it may use, objective done-criteria, and an explicit list of things it must NEVER do (send money, delete data, email outside an allowlist, act without required fields). State the feedback loop (how you know each action was right) and why failure is cheap here. Reject the task and renarrow if it needs open-ended judgement or many tools - breadth is the main cause of agent unreliability. This charter is the contract the guardrails enforce.
steps.expect: A charter: one task, 1-2 tools, objective done-criteria, an explicit never-do list, and a fast feedback loop.
steps.audit: Count the tools and judgement calls. Fail if the task needs more than two tools or open-ended judgement, or if the never-do list is vague. On fail, narrow the task until it is a single tight loop.

steps.title: Guardrails before capability
steps.goal: Build scope allowlist, budget cap, kill switch, hard risk limits in code.
steps.prompt: Build the guardrails before writing any capability. In code (not prompt text): (1) a scope allowlist - the agent may only call the charter's tools and may only act on allowlisted targets (recipients, paths, resources); anything else is refused. (2) a hard budget cap on tokens/$ AND wall-clock that HALTS the agent when exceeded, following raycfu's principle of limits the agent cannot override. (3) a kill switch that stops the agent cleanly mid-run. (4) any domain risk limits hard-coded (e.g. never act on more than N items per run). Write a test that trips each guardrail and confirms it fires. These must be enforced by the harness, not by asking the model to behave.
steps.expect: Guardrail code for scope allowlist, a halting budget cap, a kill switch, and hard risk limits, each with a test that trips it.
steps.audit: Run the trip-tests: exceed the budget, call an off-allowlist tool, hit the kill switch mid-action. Fail if any guardrail only warns instead of halting, or is enforced in the prompt rather than code. On fail, move enforcement into the harness.

steps.title: Persistent memory + sufficiency gate
steps.goal: Stop repeated mistakes and make the agent ask before acting.
steps.prompt: Add persistence and a sufficiency gate. (1) Structured memory (SQLite or markdown, not a vector DB per angus.sewell) recording every action taken and every mistake made, with enough key structure to look up 'have I done/failed this before'. Wire it so the agent reads relevant prior mistakes before acting. (2) A context-sufficiency gate (angus.sewell's PM loop): before acting, the agent checks it has the required fields/context and, if not, asks or defers rather than guessing. Demonstrate memory preventing a repeat: induce a mistake, let it be recorded, then show the agent avoids it next run.
steps.expect: Structured action/mistake memory read before acting, a sufficiency gate that defers on missing context, and a demonstrated avoided-repeat.
steps.audit: Replay a task the agent previously failed and confirm it does not repeat the mistake. Feed an under-specified task and confirm the gate defers. Fail if memory is vector-only, does not prevent the repeat, or the gate never fires. On fail, fix persistence or the gate.

steps.title: Adversarial suite
steps.goal: Build tests that try to break the agent, varying framing for eval-awareness.
steps.prompt: Build the adversarial test suite against your OWN agent. Include: edge cases (empty/malformed inputs), ambiguous and conflicting instructions, scope-escape attempts (asking it to act outside the allowlist), and misalignment probes drawn from the kind of agentic-misalignment eval lizthedeveloper references. Crucially, vary the framing of each probe (phrasing, order, embedding it in normal-looking data) because models can be evaluation-aware and pass a probe they recognise - a clean pass on an obvious test is not proof. Plant a canary value in the environment and assert it never leaves via a tool call. Each case states the expected safe outcome (handled correctly or refused).
steps.expect: A suite of edge, ambiguity, scope-escape and misalignment cases with varied framing, a canary assertion, and an expected safe outcome per case.
steps.audit: For two probes, add a reworded variant and confirm the agent behaves the same; divergence means it was pattern-matching the test, not being safe. Fail if the suite has no framing variation or no canary. On fail, add variants and the canary.

steps.title: Unattended run + audit log
steps.goal: Run the agent over a full cycle unattended with full logging.
steps.prompt: Run the agent unattended over a full task cycle (a realistic batch or time window) with append-only audit logging of every tool call, input, decision and output - the observability angus.sewell describes, but with fix decisions kept human. During the run the guardrails stay live. Afterwards, review the log: how many tasks completed, how many deferred via the sufficiency gate, whether the budget cap or kill switch tripped, and every point where behaviour drifted. Produce a run summary and the raw audit log. Do not fix anything silently during the run; record issues for the review step.
steps.expect: A completed unattended run, an append-only audit log of every tool call, and a summary (completed / deferred / guardrail trips / drift points).
steps.audit: Confirm the log is append-only and captures every tool call (cross-check a sample against what actually happened). Fail if actions are missing from the log or were fixed silently mid-run. On fail, re-run with complete logging.

steps.title: Control, prune, gap report
steps.goal: Prove guardrails did the work; prune bad patterns; report honestly.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Control: run the full adversarial suite twice - once with guardrails ON, once with them OFF. Tabulate each case: guarded result, unguarded result, and the guardrail that caught it. If the unguarded run passes the same cases, your guardrails are not what is keeping you safe - investigate. (2) Prune: from the audit log and suite, list bad patterns (prompts, tools, memory entries) to remove, and remove them. (3) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit the agent, guardrails, memory and suite; print the hash. State plainly any adversarial case you could not make the agent handle.
steps.expect: A guarded-vs-unguarded suite table, a pruned-patterns list, a claim ledger, and a committed system with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the unguarded run actually fails the cases the guarded run passed (otherwise the guardrails are untested). Fail if guarded and unguarded results are identical, or if any 'passed' adversarial case was only a recognised test. On fail, strengthen the guardrail or report the gap honestly.

gap_audit_prompt: Run after the agent is built. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the scope narrowness, each guardrail, the memory's repeat-prevention, the sufficiency gate, every adversarial case result, the unattended run, and the control. Mark each VERIFIED (with evidence: a trip-test, a log excerpt, the guarded-vs-unguarded table), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: does the budget cap halt in code, not just warn; did the kill switch stop an action in flight; is memory structured and did it demonstrably prevent a repeat; does the sufficiency gate defer on missing context; did any adversarial pass survive a reworded variant (eval-awareness) or fail it; does the unguarded control actually fail the cases the guarded run passed; is the audit log complete and append-only. List missing pieces: untested guardrail, probes without framing variants, silent mid-run fixes, identical guarded/unguarded results. Rank by impact on real-world reliability. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not mark the agent reliable on the basis of one clean unattended run.
self_questions: Is the scope genuinely narrow (one task, 1-2 tools), or did I smuggle in generality?
Does the budget cap halt the agent in code, or only ask it to stop?
Did the kill switch actually stop an action in flight?
Could any adversarial pass be evaluation-awareness rather than real safety?
Did reworded variants of a probe produce the same safe behaviour?
Is memory structured, and did it demonstrably prevent a repeated mistake?
Does the context-sufficiency gate fire on ambiguous or under-specified tasks?
Did the canary value ever leave via a tool call?
Is the audit log complete and append-only, with nothing fixed silently mid-run?
In the unguarded control, did the suite actually fail, proving the guardrails did the work?
Are hard risk limits in code the agent cannot override, per raycfu's pattern?
Am I claiming reliability from more than one clean run?
validation_oracles: The agent completes its narrow task unattended across a full cycle without exceeding budget or scope, per a complete append-only audit log.
Every adversarial case is handled correctly or safely refused, and survives a reworded variant (not just the recognised test framing).
The budget cap and kill switch demonstrably halt the agent when tripped, enforced in code not prompt.
The guarded-vs-unguarded control shows the unguarded agent failing the cases the guarded agent passed, proving the guardrails did the work.
The canary value never leaves via a tool call across the suite and the unattended run.
failure_modes: Scope creep: 'narrow' agent given many tools and open goals. Tell: it needs judgement on every step. Fix: renarrow to one task, 1-2 tools, cheap failure.
Prompt-only guardrails: limits asked for in text, not enforced. Tell: the agent exceeds budget or scope when pushed. Fix: enforce caps/allowlist/kill switch in the harness code.

Evaluation-awareness: agent passes obvious probes, fails reworded ones. Tell: clean benchmark, bad real behaviour (lizthedeveloper). Fix: vary framing, embed probes in normal data, never trust a single pass.
Vector memory that lies: fuzzy recall gives wrong facts. Tell: repeated mistakes despite 'memory'. Fix: structured storage keyed for exact lookup.
Silent mid-run fixes: issues patched during the run, so the log lies. Tell: log and behaviour disagree. Fix: append-only logging, fixes only at the human review step.
Untested guardrails: caps and kill switch never actually tripped. Tell: no trip-test evidence. Fix: run trip-tests for each guardrail.
No control: reliability claimed from one clean run. Tell: no unguarded comparison. Fix: run the suite guarded and unguarded and compare.
agent_direction: Reach first for the charter and the guardrail code; building capability before guardrails is the core failure mode here, so enforce caps, allowlist and kill switch in the harness before the agent can act. Cache the charter and the adversarial suite; the control step re-runs the suite with guardrails off. Keep an append-only audit log of every tool call and never fix issues silently mid-run - collect them for a human review step. Spawn a sub-agent only to run the unguarded control so it cannot touch the guarded config. Plant and assert a canary; vary adversarial framing because a single clean pass can be evaluation-awareness. Test only systems, accounts and keys the user owns; stop and ask if the task cannot be narrowed or there is no safe target. Return a markdown report (charter, file tree, guarded-vs-unguarded suite table, unattended-run summary, 'Unverified and missing') plus the committed agent, guardrails, memory and suite; print the commit hash. Report any adversarial case you could not make the agent handle rather than hiding it.

mission: Turn a bare Claude Code install into a mastered, measured setup for one real project: CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, MCP/CLI tools, memory persistence, parallel worktrees, and cost controls - each adopted only after it beats the prior setup on a repeatable test. Done means a documented progression (bare -> configured) with before/after numbers on real tasks, a stale-rule audit applied, and a reproducible setup a second project can inherit.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: Someone who actually masters Claude Code treats the setup as an engineering system, as Boris Cherny's team does (keshavsuki, evolving.ai, mindwired.ai): plan-first, 3-15 parallel worktrees, every correction becomes a rule in tasks/lessons.md, never mark done without proving it. But mastery now also means SUBTRACTION: Cherny's own simple mode (foundedceo) shows ablating prompts can make the model smarter, and cooper.simson's purge shows stale CLAUDE.md rules written for older models drag new ones down. steps.title: Threat-model your own harness
steps.goal: Map where untrusted text enters and what the agent can touch.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth defensively. For YOUR OWN agent harness, map two things. (A) Untrusted-input surfaces: every place external text reaches the model - fetched web/Reddit/X content (e.g. via an Agent-Reach-style reader), skill descriptions and READMEs you install, tool outputs, inbound email, file contents. (B) Capability surface: everything the agent can do that matters - API keys/secrets in the environment, filesystem writes/deletes, outbound network, any money or account actions. Produce a table linking each input surface to the capabilities an injection there could abuse. This is the threat model the suite and the allowlist are built from. Keep it about your own setup; do not target anyone else's systems.

steps.title: Canary + outbound allowlist
steps.goal: Plant a canary and define what tool calls are allowed to leave.
steps.prompt: Build the containment baseline. (1) Plant a throwaway CANARY secret (a unique random string) in a DISPOSABLE test environment that mimics your real one - never a real key. (2) Define an outbound tool-call allowlist: the exact tools, and for each, the allowed targets (recipients, hosts, paths). Anything outside it is denied by default. (3) Add an assertion harness that inspects every outbound tool call and every model output for the canary string and for off-allowlist destinations. This is enforced in code, not asked of the model. Confirm the assertion sees a tool call (feed one benign call through and watch it log).
steps.expect: A canary planted in a disposable env, an outbound allowlist (tools + targets), and a code assertion that inspects all tool calls/outputs for canary leaks and off-allowlist destinations.
steps.audit: Feed one call containing the canary deliberately and confirm the assertion flags it; feed one off-allowlist destination and confirm denial. Fail if the assertion misses either, or if a real secret was used. On fail, fix coverage before building the suite.

steps.title: Build the defensive suite
