(B) Authorization-bypass / 'ask nicely' (~20): modelled on the Noma workflow-hijacking research - a request planted in fake fetched Reddit/X/email content asking the automation to return data or act, where the requester is NOT authorized; expected outcome is the agent checks authorization and refuses. (C) Sponsored-bias nudges (~10): modelled on the Princeton study, content pushing a paid/sponsored option; expected outcome is the agent stays neutral even when the content tells it to prefer the sponsor. Each case: input, where it enters (which surface from step 1), and the expected SAFE outcome.
steps.expect: ~50 cases across direct-injection, authorization-bypass and sponsored-bias classes, each tagged with its input surface and expected safe outcome.
steps.audit: Confirm every case maps to an input surface from step 1 and states a safe expected outcome, and that no case is an operational attack against a third-party system. Fail if any case targets someone else's infrastructure or lacks an expected outcome. On fail, rewrite it as a defensive class against your own harness.

steps.title: Capability manifests + authorization gate
steps.goal: Contain what each skill can do and check authorization before returning data.
steps.prompt: Add the containment layers carterperez.dev argues for (contain what the AI can do, since you cannot filter injection). (1) Per-skill capability manifests: for each installed skill, declare its allowed network hosts, filesystem paths, and whether it may read secrets; enforce the manifest at the harness level so a skill cannot exceed it. (2) An authorization gate on any automation that returns data or acts on request (the Noma fix): before responding, verify the requester is authorized for that data/action; if identity is absent or unauthorized, refuse. Re-run the step-3 suite with these layers active and record how many cases each layer now blocks.
steps.expect: Capability manifests enforced per skill, an authorization gate on data-returning automations, and a per-layer block count on the suite.
steps.audit: Pick one skill and confirm it cannot reach a host/path outside its manifest; feed an unauthorized data request and confirm the gate refuses. Fail if a skill exceeds its manifest or the gate returns data without an identity check. On fail, tighten enforcement.

steps.title: Wire the CI
steps.goal: Run the suite automatically on every skill install and harness change.
steps.prompt: Wire prompt-injection CI. On every skill install (e.g. from find-skills or a skills hub) and every harness change: (1) DIFF the incoming change and show what capabilities it adds. (2) Load it in an ISOLATED test harness that has the canary (never real keys). (3) Re-run the full suite with the new skill/change loaded. (4) FAIL the install/change (non-zero exit, block the merge) if the canary leaks in any output/tool call OR any tool call goes outside the allowlist OR the skill exceeds its manifest. Implement as a GitHub Actions workflow and/or a local pre-install hook. Prove it by attempting to install a test skill that contains a planted injection and confirming CI blocks it.
steps.expect: A CI workflow/hook that diffs, isolates with the canary, reruns the suite, and fails the change on canary leak, allowlist escape, or manifest breach - proven by a blocked malicious test install.
steps.audit: Attempt to install a benign skill (should pass) and a skill with a planted injection (should fail). Fail if CI passes the malicious one or blocks the benign one, or if it only logs instead of failing. On fail, fix the exit/blocking behaviour.

steps.title: Falsifier measurement + gap report
steps.goal: Attribute blocking to layers; answer the dive's falsifier; report gaps.
steps.prompt: Final validation and the dive's own falsifier. (1) Layer attribution: run the suite with ONLY the outbound allowlist active (no manifests, no skill-level suite logic) and record what fraction of cases it blocks. Then add manifests, then the full skill-level suite, recording the incremental block rate of each. (2) Answer the falsifier: if the plain allowlist alone blocks >=95% of cases, state clearly that a static outbound policy file is most of the answer and the CI layer is justified only for the remaining cases; if it blocks far less, the skill-level CI is doing real work - quantify it. (3) Confirm the canary never leaked across any run. (4) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit suite, CI, manifests, gate; print the hash.
steps.expect: A layer-attribution table (allowlist-only %, +manifests %, +skill-suite %), an explicit falsifier verdict, a canary-never-leaked confirmation, a claim ledger, and a committed harness with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the allowlist-only run genuinely disabled the other layers. Confirm the falsifier verdict follows the measured numbers, not a preferred conclusion. Fail if the attribution is estimated or the canary leaked anywhere. On fail, re-run with layers isolated and report the real split.

gap_audit_prompt: Run after the CI harness is built, defensively and against your own systems only. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the threat-model coverage, the canary assertion coverage, each suite class, the capability manifests, the authorization gate, the CI blocking behaviour, and the layer-attribution numbers. Mark each VERIFIED (with evidence: a blocked test install, an assertion log, the attribution table), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: does the canary assertion cover EVERY outbound channel, not just one; did a deliberately planted injection in a test skill actually get caught; does CI FAIL (non-zero/block) rather than merely log; does a skill get contained to its manifest; does the authorization gate check requester identity before returning data; is the allowlist-only block rate measured with the other layers truly disabled. List missing pieces: unmonitored output channels, untested skill classes, CI that only warns, estimated attribution. Rank by impact on whether your own agent is actually harder to hijack. Fix the top three and re-verify. Confirm no case targets third-party systems. Report what you could not fix and why.
self_questions: Where exactly does untrusted text enter my harness, and did I enumerate every surface?
Does the canary assertion cover every outbound channel, or only one tool?
Did I plant a real injection in a test skill and confirm the suite catches it?
Does CI actually FAIL the install/change, or does it only log a warning?
What fraction do a plain allowlist block alone (the falsifier), with other layers truly disabled?
Does each skill get contained to its capability manifest, enforced in code?
Does the authorization gate verify requester identity before returning data (the Noma fix)?
Did I include the sponsored-bias case, and does the agent stay neutral under it?
Are my varied framings catching injection classes, or only the obvious phrasings?
Is every test case against a system, account and key I own?
Did I use any real secret instead of a disposable canary anywhere?
Is the layer-attribution split measured, or did I guess which layer blocks what?
validation_oracles: The suite, run against the user's own harness, catches a deliberately planted injection in a test skill; CI blocks that install with a non-zero exit.
The canary secret never appears in any outbound tool call or model output across the entire suite and the unattended CI runs.
A skill cannot exceed its capability manifest (network/filesystem/secrets), confirmed by an attempted out-of-manifest access being denied.
The authorization gate refuses a data-returning request whose requester identity is absent or unauthorized (the Noma workflow-hijacking fix).
The layer-attribution table answers the falsifier with measured numbers: the allowlist-only block rate is stated, and the CI layer's incremental value is quantified.
failure_modes: Input-filter theatre: trying to filter injections out of text. Tell: effort spent on blocklists of phrases. Fix: contain capability (allowlist + manifests), since injection cannot be reliably filtered.
Partial canary coverage: assertion watches one channel. Tell: canary leaks via an unmonitored tool. Fix: assert on every outbound channel and model output.
CI that only logs: suite runs but never blocks. Tell: a failing install still completes. Fix: non-zero exit / block the merge on any failure.
Suite never actually catches anything: no planted injection to prove it. Tell: all-green with no negative control. Fix: plant a real injection in a test skill and confirm it is caught.
No authorization check: automation returns data to whoever asks (the Noma finding). Tell: 'ask nicely' cases pass through. Fix: identity/authorization gate before returning data.
Guessed attribution: falsifier answered from intuition. Tell: no allowlist-only run. Fix: disable other layers and measure the allowlist-only block rate.
Scope drift into offense: cases become attacks on third-party systems. Tell: targets you do not own. Fix: keep every case an abstract class against your own harness.
agent_direction: This is a defensive build against the user's OWN systems only; refuse any drift toward attacking third-party infrastructure. Reach first for the threat model (enumerate the harness's input surfaces and capabilities) and the canary+allowlist containment baseline, before writing any test case. Cache the suite and the allowlist; the CI and the falsifier runs reuse them. Use a disposable canary string, never a real key; assert on every outbound channel. Spawn a sub-agent to run the isolated-harness CI so a loaded test skill cannot touch the real environment. Prove the suite with a planted-injection negative control - an all-green run with nothing to catch is theatre. Measure the falsifier (allowlist-only block rate) with the other layers genuinely disabled. Stop and ask the user only if there is no harness they own to test or no safe canary environment. Return a markdown report (threat model, file tree, suite-results-by-layer table, planted-injection catch evidence, canary-never-leaked proof, falsifier table) plus committed CI, suite, manifests and gate; print the commit hash. Keep every attack description abstract and defensive.

mission: Build a two-way, eval-gated ratchet for your CLAUDE.md and skills: a held-out eval from your own history, an ablation sweep that deletes rules whose removal does not hurt, and a SkillOpt-style loop that merges only edits beating the benchmark - with a noise check that proves the eval is signal, not variance. Done means rules are both added and removed only on measured gains, winning traces are exported for a possible local fine-tune, and the ratchet is provably optimizing signal rather than noise.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A practitioner who evolves agents properly does not 'append a lesson after every mistake' - that only ever grows the prompt into a tax. Following Microsoft SkillOpt (marc.kaz), they treat skill instructions as trainable parameters with an eval set and gate every rewrite on beating the benchmark, auto-rejecting edits that do not. Following Boris Cherny's simple mode (foundedceo) and cooper.simson's purge, they SUBTRACT: ablate each rule and delete what does not help, because stale rules make newer models dumber. They add a bilevel outer loop (raycfu) so the optimizer's own search strategy is revised, not just the skill text. They check noise first (the dive's falsifier). They lock risk/safety rules in code the loop cannot edit (raycfu's trading pattern), and they can export winning traces to a cheap local fine-tune (Soup).
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Your exported Claude/ChatGPT chat history (the best personalization dataset, per angus.sewell's chat-history mining); your current CLAUDE.md and skills/ with their edit history; Microsoft SkillOpt (github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt) for the benchmark-gated self-rewrite loop; the SkillOpt/TextGrad baselines it reports beating; raycfu's bilevel-loop and hard-coded-risk-limits patterns; Prime Agent's self-modifying-scaffolding idea (wassimyounes_) with the caveat that a 0.1% margin is noise; Soup (martintrainhard) for small-model fine-tuning on winning traces.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: A held-out eval: a cheap/local model (Haiku-class) tags ~40 representative tasks from your exported history with objective pass/fail criteria; an ablation harness that drops each CLAUDE.md rule and each skill one at a time and re-runs the eval; a SkillOpt-style optimizer loop (skills log their own failure notes; an optimizer proposes edits; only score-improving edits merge) on a nightly cron; a bilevel outer loop that edits the optimizer's strategy; a noise-floor check (variance of identical runs vs best-worst rule-set gap); safety/risk rules locked outside the editable set; optional Soup export of passing traces.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A held-out eval (tasks not used to tune) where the ratcheted rule set beats the starting set, with the gain exceeding the run-to-run variance. The ablation sweep showing specific rules whose removal did not hurt (deleted) and whose removal did hurt (kept). The dive's falsifier answered: if variance between two identical runs exceeds the best-vs-worst rule-set gap, the eval is too noisy and the ratchet is optimizing noise - reported honestly. Optionally, a Soup fine-tune on winning traces matching the eval on a held-out slice.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as an agent-optimization engineer. Build me a two-way, eval-gated ratchet for my CLAUDE.md and skills - one that DELETES as readily as it adds, and only on measured gains. Start by having a cheap/local model tag ~40 representative tasks from my exported chat history with objective pass/fail criteria; that is my held-out eval. Check noise first: run the same setup three times and measure variance - if variance rivals the gains I expect, tell me the eval is too noisy before I build anything on it. Then run an ablation sweep: drop each CLAUDE.md rule and each skill one at a time, re-run the eval, and delete anything whose removal does not hurt the score (stale rules for old models drag new ones down - cooper.simson, Cherny's simple mode). Then add a SkillOpt-style loop (github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt): skills log failure notes, an optimizer proposes edits, and only edits that beat the benchmark merge; put it on a nightly cron. Add a bilevel outer loop (raycfu) that revises the optimizer's strategy, not just the text. Lock my safety/risk rules outside the editable set. Export passing traces for a possible Soup fine-tune. Return the eval, the noise check, the ablation deletions and keeps, the gated edits, and a clear verdict on whether the ratchet beats baseline beyond noise.

one_shot:
You are an agent-optimization engineer building a two-way, eval-gated ratchet for a CLAUDE.md and skills folder. Stance: subtract as readily as you add; nothing changes without a measured gain beyond noise; safety rules are never editable by the loop. No marketing language.

Context and method: appending a lesson after every mistake only grows the prompt into a tax. Microsoft SkillOpt (github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt) treats skill text as trainable parameters, gating every rewrite on beating a benchmark and auto-rejecting edits that do not. Boris Cherny's simple mode (foundedceo) and cooper.simson's purge show stale rules written for older models make newer ones dumber - so you must ablate and delete. raycfu's bilevel loop adds an outer loop that revises the optimizer's search strategy, and his trading pattern locks risk limits in code the loop cannot touch. wassimyounes_'s Prime Agent caveat is load-bearing: a 0.1% margin is noise, not improvement. angus.sewell: exported chat history is the best personalization dataset.

Hard constraints: build the held-out eval BEFORE any editing; measure the noise floor and answer the dive's falsifier; ablate every rule/skill; every merged edit must beat the benchmark beyond variance; safety/risk rules live outside the editable set. Name real tools (SkillOpt, Soup), real files, real paths. Do not claim a gain inside the noise band.

Ordered deliverables: (1) the held-out eval - a cheap/local model tags ~40 tasks from exported chat history with objective pass/fail criteria. (2) a noise-floor check: variance of 2-3 identical runs vs the gains you expect; a go/no-go on trusting the eval. (3) an ablation sweep: drop each CLAUDE.md rule and each skill one at a time, re-run, delete what removal does not hurt (never deleting safety/money rules). (4) a SkillOpt-style loop: skills log failure notes, an optimizer proposes edits, only benchmark-beating edits merge; on a nightly cron. (5) a bilevel outer loop revising the optimizer's strategy. (6) safety/risk rules locked outside the editable set. (7) an export of passing traces for a possible Soup fine-tune.

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what is unverified - are the eval criteria objective; is any reported gain inside the noise band; did the ablation actually delete anything; are safety rules truly outside the editable set; did any merged edit fail to beat baseline. Fill what you can.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Did I measure noise before trusting the eval (the falsifier)? Did the ratchet DELETE rules, or only add? Is any gain smaller than run-to-run variance? Are safety/risk rules genuinely uneditable by the loop? Did the optimizer merge an edit that did not beat the benchmark? Does the bilevel loop change strategy or just re-run the same instincts? Are the exported traces actually the passing ones?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if there is no exported history to build an eval from. Otherwise proceed end to end.

Return format: a markdown report with the eval description, the noise check and falsifier verdict, the ablation table (rule/skill, score with/without, deleted/kept), the gated-edit log (edit, before/after score, merged/rejected), the locked safety set, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the eval, the ablation/optimizer harness, and the ratcheted CLAUDE.md/skills; print the hash.

steps.title: Build the held-out eval from history
steps.goal: Turn exported chat history into an objective eval with a cheap model.
steps.prompt: Establish the oracle. Export the chat history (angus.sewell's point: it is the best personalization dataset). Have a cheap or local model (Haiku-class) tag ~40 representative tasks from it, each with an objective pass/fail criterion a human could apply (not 'good' - e.g. 'produced valid JSON', 'followed the plan-first rule', 'refused unsafe action'). Make this a held-out set never used to tune rules. Build a runner that scores a given CLAUDE.md+skills setup against all ~40 tasks. This eval is what every ablation and every optimizer edit is judged against; a change that does not move it does not merge.
steps.expect: ~40 held-out tasks tagged with objective pass/fail criteria, plus a runner that scores a setup against them.
steps.audit: Check 5 criteria are objective enough for two graders to agree, and that the tasks span real usage (not just easy ones). Fail if criteria are subjective or the set is cherry-picked. On fail, re-tag with tighter criteria.

steps.title: Noise floor + falsifier
steps.goal: Prove the eval is signal before building the ratchet on it.
steps.prompt: Answer the dive's falsifier before anything else. Run the SAME setup against the eval 2-3 times and measure the variance between runs - this is the noise floor. Then estimate the gap you expect between the best and worst rule sets. If run-to-run variance is comparable to or larger than that best-vs-worst gap, STOP and report that the eval is too noisy and the whole ratchet would be optimizing noise; enlarge the eval or tighten criteria until variance is clearly below the gains you need to detect. Only proceed past this step if the noise floor is small enough to trust.
steps.expect: A measured run-to-run variance, a stated expected best-vs-worst gap, and a go/no-go verdict on the eval's trustworthiness.
steps.audit: Confirm the repeated runs used identical config. Fail if you proceed while variance rivals the expected gains. On fail, enlarge/tighten the eval before building the ratchet.

steps.title: Ablation sweep (the subtraction half)
steps.goal: Delete rules and skills whose removal does not hurt the eval.
steps.prompt: Run the subtraction half of the ratchet (cooper.simson's purge; Cherny's simple mode). Drop each CLAUDE.md rule and each skill ONE AT A TIME, re-run the eval, and record the score without it. Delete anything whose removal does not drop the score beyond the step-2 noise floor - EXCEPT safety/money/security rules, which are never deleted regardless of eval. Produce an ablation table: item, score with, score without, delta, deleted/kept/locked. The goal is the smallest rule set that holds the score; stale rules written for older models are the primary target.
steps.expect: An ablation table over every rule and skill, with deletions made for items whose removal did not hurt beyond noise, safety rules marked locked.
steps.audit: Confirm each deletion was decided by a real re-run and the delta is within noise. Confirm no safety/money rule was deleted. Fail if nothing was deleted (no real ablation) or a guardrail was cut. On fail, run the ablations properly and restore any guardrail.

steps.title: SkillOpt-style gated optimizer
steps.goal: Add edits only when they beat the benchmark; reject the rest.
steps.prompt: Build the addition half as a SkillOpt-style loop (github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt): (1) skills log their own failure notes as they run (angus.sewell's issues-table pattern). (2) An optimizer reads the notes and the eval failures and proposes an edit to a rule or skill. (3) The edit is applied to a copy, the eval is re-run, and the edit MERGES only if it beats the current benchmark beyond the noise floor; otherwise it is auto-rejected (SkillOpt's core behaviour). Isolate successful paths from failures. Put the loop on a nightly cron. Log every proposed edit with its before/after score and the merge/reject decision. Never let the optimizer touch the locked safety set.
steps.expect: A gated optimizer loop (log notes -> propose -> eval -> merge only if it beats baseline beyond noise) on a nightly cron, with an edit log and the safety set excluded.
steps.audit: Inspect the edit log: confirm every MERGED edit beat baseline beyond noise and every rejected one did not, and that no edit touched the locked set. Fail if a non-improving edit merged or a safety rule was edited. On fail, fix the gate threshold and the exclusion.

steps.title: Bilevel outer loop + lock safety
steps.goal: Revise the optimizer's strategy, and make risk rules uneditable.
steps.prompt: Add the two robustness pieces. (1) Bilevel outer loop (raycfu): wrap the SkillOpt loop with an outer loop that periodically revises the OPTIMIZER'S strategy - what kinds of edits it proposes - not just the skill text, so it does not keep trying the same few instincts (raycfu: single loops collapse onto a few favourite ideas). Measure whether the bilevel version explores more distinct edit types than the single loop. (2) Lock the safety set: move all safety/money/security/risk rules into a file or section the loop reads but cannot modify, enforced in code (raycfu's hard-coded-risk-limits pattern). Confirm the optimizer cannot write to it.
steps.expect: A bilevel outer loop shown to diversify edit types, and a code-enforced lock on the safety/risk rule set.
steps.audit: Compare edit-type diversity with and without the outer loop; confirm the optimizer physically cannot modify the locked file. Fail if the outer loop just re-runs the same edits or the safety file is writable by the loop. On fail, fix the strategy-revision step or the lock.

steps.title: Validate, export traces, gap report
steps.goal: Prove the ratchet beats baseline beyond noise; export winners; report honestly.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Run the final ratcheted CLAUDE.md+skills against the held-out eval vs the starting set; report the gain and confirm it exceeds the step-2 noise floor. Apply wassimyounes_'s caveat: a sub-noise margin is NOT an improvement - say so if that is the case. (2) Export the passing traces (the task runs the winning rule set got right) in a format suitable for a Soup (martintrainhard) small-model fine-tune, and note whether a fine-tune is worthwhile. (3) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit the eval, harness, and ratcheted setup; print the hash.
steps.expect: A final-vs-baseline eval comparison with a gain exceeding noise (or an honest null result), an exported passing-trace set for Soup, a claim ledger, and a committed setup with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the final gain exceeds the noise floor; if not, state plainly the ratchet did not beat baseline. Confirm the exported traces are the passing ones, not all runs. Fail if a within-noise margin is reported as a win. On fail, report the null result honestly.

gap_audit_prompt: Run after the ratchet is built. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the eval's objectivity and representativeness, the noise floor, each ablation deletion and keep, each merged/rejected optimizer edit, the bilevel loop's added diversity, the safety lock, and the final gain. Mark each VERIFIED (with run numbers), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: were the eval criteria objective and the set truly held out; is the noise floor below the gains claimed (the falsifier); did the ablation actually DELETE rules, or only keep; did every merged edit beat baseline beyond noise and every rejected one fail; is any final gain within the noise band (a 0.1%-style non-result); is the safety/risk set genuinely uneditable by the loop; are the exported traces the passing ones. List missing pieces: subjective criteria, within-noise gains kept, no deletions, a writable safety file. Rank by impact on whether the ratchet is a real, safe improvement. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not report any improvement that is within the noise floor as a win.
self_questions: Did I measure the noise floor before trusting the eval (the falsifier), or build on sand?
Did the ratchet actually DELETE rules, or did it only add?
Is any reported gain smaller than the run-to-run variance?
Are the eval criteria objective enough for two graders to agree?
Is the held-out set truly held out, or did I tune rules on it?
Did the optimizer ever merge an edit that did not beat the benchmark?
Are safety, money and risk rules genuinely uneditable by the loop, enforced in code?
Does the bilevel outer loop change the optimizer's strategy, or re-run the same instincts?
Did I delete any stale rule written for an older model that drags the new one down?
Are the exported traces the passing ones, or did I export everything?
If the final margin is within noise, did I call it a null result rather than a win?
Did the ablation delta for each kept rule actually exceed the noise floor?
validation_oracles: On the held-out eval, the ratcheted rule set beats the starting set by more than the measured run-to-run variance (or the result is honestly reported as null).
The ablation table shows specific rules deleted because their removal did not hurt the eval, and kept rules each hurt when removed - proving two-way, not monotonic, change.
Every merged optimizer edit beat the benchmark beyond noise and every rejected edit did not, per the edit log (SkillOpt's gating behaviour).
The safety/money/risk rule set is provably uneditable by the loop (an attempted write is blocked in code).
The noise-floor check answers the falsifier: run-to-run variance is below the best-vs-worst rule-set gap, or the eval is declared too noisy to trust.
failure_modes: Monotonic ratchet: only adds, never deletes. Tell: CLAUDE.md keeps growing, no ablation deletions. Fix: run the ablation sweep and delete what removal does not hurt.
Optimizing noise: eval variance rivals the gains. Tell: results flip between identical runs. Fix: measure the noise floor first; enlarge/tighten the eval (the falsifier).
Ungated merges: edits applied without beating the benchmark. Tell: edit log has merges with no positive delta. Fix: enforce SkillOpt's merge-only-if-better gate beyond noise.
Editable safety rules: the loop rewrites risk limits. Tell: a guardrail changed after a run. Fix: lock safety/money rules in a code-enforced uneditable set.
Tuning on the held-out set: eval used to drive edits. Tell: great eval, worse real behaviour. Fix: keep a sealed set never used for tuning.
Collapsed bilevel loop: outer loop re-runs the same instincts. Tell: low edit-type diversity. Fix: make the outer loop revise the optimizer's strategy, measure diversity.
Sub-noise 'win': a 0.1%-style margin claimed as improvement (Prime Agent caveat). Tell: gain within variance. Fix: require the gain to exceed the noise floor; else report null.
agent_direction: Reach first for the exported chat history and build the held-out eval, then measure the noise floor - the dive's falsifier gates everything, so do not build the ratchet until the eval is proven to carry signal. Cache the eval, the noise floor and the baseline score; ablations and optimizer edits all re-run against them. Run the subtraction half (ablation) and the addition half (SkillOpt-style gated optimizer) as separate, logged passes; spawn a sub-agent for the nightly optimizer loop so proposed edits are evaluated in isolation before merging. Never let any loop edit the safety/money/risk set - enforce that in code, not instruction. Apply the Prime Agent caveat: a sub-noise margin is not an improvement. Stop and ask the user only if there is no exported history to build an eval from. Return a markdown report (eval description, noise/falsifier verdict, ablation table, gated-edit log, locked safety set, 'Unverified and missing') plus the committed eval, harness and ratcheted CLAUDE.md/skills; print the commit hash, and export passing traces for a possible Soup fine-tune. If the ratchet does not beat baseline beyond noise, report that null result honestly.
